items.stem: Which research method best describes the study by Yuille and Cutshall (1986) on real eyewitnesses to a shooting?
options: questionnaire survey
field experiment
ethnographic participant observation
case study
items.answer: case study
items.markingKey: D. Yuille and Cutshall (1986): 13 of 21 witnesses to a fatal shooting in Vancouver were interviewed 4-5 months later, including two misleading questions; accounts were compared with the original police interviews and evidence.

items.stem: Explain how the findings of Yuille and Cutshall (1986) provide evidence about the reliability of eyewitness memory in real-life settings.
items.answer: Findings: witnesses remained highly accurate after several months and were not misled by the leading questions; those most distressed at the time were among the most accurate. Link: these results are evidence about the reliability of eyewitness memory in real-life settings.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for accurate findings (witnesses remained highly accurate after several months and were not misled by the leading questions; those most distressed at the time were among the most accurate); remaining marks for explicitly explaining what the findings show about the reliability of eyewitness memory in real-life settings (not just restating them).

items.stem: Explain how leading questions can distort eyewitness testimony.
items.answer: A leading question introduces post-event information (e.g. "smashed") that either biases the response or alters the stored memory itself, so the witness reconstructs the event in line with the question - as shown by more false reports of broken glass in Loftus and Palmer (1974).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A leading question introduces post-event information (e.g. "smashed") that either biases the response or alters the stored memory itself, so the witness reconstructs the event in line with the question - as shown by more false reports of broken glass in Loftus and Palmer (1974). (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: At an accident in Lima, an officer asks a witness, "Did you see the car run the red light?" The question presupposes the car ran the light, which may bias the witness's answer or alter the memory itself

items.stem: With reference to Loftus and Palmer (1974), explain how research has investigated reconstructive memory and the effect of leading questions.
items.answer: Loftus and Palmer (1974). Aim: to investigate whether the wording of a question affects eyewitness estimates of speed and memory of an event. Method: Experiment 1: 45 students watched clips of car accidents and were asked how fast the cars were going when they "smashed", "collided", "bumped", "hit" or "contacted" each other. Experiment 2: 150 students were asked with "smashed", "hit" or no speed question, and a week later asked if they had seen broken glass. Findings: speed estimates were highest for "smashed" (40.8 mph) and lowest for "contacted" (31.8 mph); in experiment 2, 16/50 "smashed" participants reported broken glass compared with 7/50 for "hit" and 6/50 controls Link: reconstructive memory and the effect of leading questions.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: speed estimates were highest for "smashed" (40.8 mph) and lowest for "contacted" (31.8 mph); in experiment 2, 16/50 "smashed" participants reported broken glass compared with 7/50 for "hit" and 6/50 controls); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to reconstructive memory and the effect of leading questions. A study that is described but not linked cannot score more than half marks.

items.stem: A student claims: "Confident eyewitnesses are always accurate." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Confidence can be inflated by feedback and repeated questioning; DNA exonerations (the Innocence Project) show many confident witnesses were wrong.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Eyewitness testimony is too unreliable to be used in court."
items.answer: Eyewitness testimony can be accurate under the right conditions; it should be used with caution, good interview practice and corroborating evidence.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: leading questions (Loftus and Palmer, 1974); false memories (Loftus and Pickrell, 1995); DNA exonerations. Arguments against: real witnesses can be accurate (Yuille and Cutshall, 1986); lab studies lack ecological validity; the cognitive interview improves accuracy. Supported judgement: Eyewitness testimony can be accurate under the right conditions; it should be used with caution, good interview practice and corroborating evidence.

items.stem: Using Loftus and Pickrell (1995) as supporting evidence, explain the creation of false memories through suggestion.
items.answer: Loftus and Pickrell (1995). Aim: to investigate whether a false memory of a childhood event can be implanted. items.stem: Explain how the framing effect can influence decision-making.

items.stem: Describe the study by Brown and Kulik (1977) and explain what it shows about the role of emotion and personal significance in flashbulb memory.
items.answer: Brown and Kulik (1977). Aim: to investigate whether people have especially vivid memories of surprising, consequential events. items.stem: "Flashbulb memories are permanent and perfectly accurate." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: They feel vivid and are held with confidence, but research shows they change over time (Neisser and Harsch, 1992).

items.stem: With reference to Yuille and Cutshall (1986), explain how research has investigated the reliability of eyewitness memory in real-life settings.
items.answer: Yuille and Cutshall (1986). Aim: to investigate the accuracy of eyewitness memory of a real crime. Method: 13 of 21 witnesses to a fatal shooting in Vancouver were interviewed 4-5 months later, including two misleading questions; accounts were compared with the original police interviews and evidence. Findings: witnesses remained highly accurate after several months and were not misled by the leading questions; those most distressed at the time were among the most accurate Link: the reliability of eyewitness memory in real-life settings.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: witnesses remained highly accurate after several months and were not misled by the leading questions; those most distressed at the time were among the most accurate); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to the reliability of eyewitness memory in real-life settings. A study that is described but not linked cannot score more than half marks.

items.stem: A government in Kuala Lumpur wants more people to register as organ donors. Using research on cognitive biases, suggest one strategy and explain why it might work.
items.answer: Use an opt-out default and gain framing ("save up to eight lives"); defaults exploit status-quo bias and System 1 thinking, and positive framing increases acceptance (Tversky and Kahneman, 1981).
items.markingKey: Use an opt-out default and gain framing ("save up to eight lives"); defaults exploit status-quo bias and System 1 thinking, and positive framing increases acceptance (Tversky and Kahneman, 1981).

items.stem: A police force in Nairobi wants to improve the accuracy of eyewitness statements. Using research, suggest two changes to interview procedures.
items.answer: Avoid leading questions (Loftus and Palmer, 1974); use the cognitive interview (context reinstatement, report everything, change order and perspective); interview soon after the event before post-event information; record interviews.

items.stem: With reference to Sharot et al. (2007), explain how research has investigated the role of the amygdala in emotional memory.
items.answer: Sharot et al. (2007). Aim: to investigate the neural basis of flashbulb memories of the 9/11 attacks. Method: About three years after 9/11, 24 participants who had been in Manhattan recalled events from that day and from the summer of 2001 while in an fMRI scanner. Findings: participants who had been close to the World Trade Center (Downtown) showed greater amygdala activation for 9/11 memories than for summer memories; those further away (Midtown) did not Link: the role of the amygdala in emotional memory.

items.stem: Using two relevant studies, discuss the claim that eyewitness testimony is too unreliable to be used in court.
items.answer: Eyewitness testimony can be accurate under the right conditions; it should be used with caution, good interview practice and corroborating evidence.

items.stem: "Human decision-making is fundamentally irrational." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Decision-making is boundedly rational: biases are real, but heuristics are often effective in real environments.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: anchoring, framing, availability biases are robust; predictable deviations from rational choice. Arguments against: heuristics are adaptive ("ecological rationality", Gigerenzer); lab problems are artificial; experts often decide well in familiar domains. Supported judgement: Decision-making is boundedly rational: biases are real, but heuristics are often effective in real environments. items.stem: Using Tversky and Kahneman (1981) as supporting evidence, explain the framing effect and loss aversion.
items.answer: Tversky and Kahneman (1981). Aim: to investigate whether the framing of options as gains or losses affects choices. items.stem: Using Talarico and Rubin (2003) as supporting evidence, explain whether flashbulb memories are more accurate than ordinary memories.
items.answer: Talarico and Rubin (2003). Aim: to compare the consistency of flashbulb memories with everyday memories over time. Method: On 12 September 2001, 54 Duke University students recorded their memory of hearing about 9/11 and of a recent everyday event; they were retested after 1, 6 or 32 weeks. Findings: consistency declined at a similar rate for both types of memory, but ratings of vividness and confidence remained high only for the 9/11 memory Link: whether flashbulb memories are more accurate than ordinary memories.
